utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we hear each other properly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please pull up your chair, relax. Could you sit comfortably, please. I told you already before we talked before this appearance of yours, I said that you should speak slowly and into the microphone when you answer questions before the Trial Chamber so that the Trial Chamber could receive a proper interpretation. Also, as I told you, could you please pause a few seconds after my question. You and I understand each other, but it is necessary for the interpretation to be correct and correctly recorded. Sir, could you please tell us your name, slowly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber when you were born?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of May, 1933, in the village of Brvnik, municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do your ancestors come from that area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your family status is? Are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm married. I have a son and a daughter. I have two granddaughters from my son and one grandson from my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber: During the war in 1992 and 1993, how old were your children? Were they of age?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My son was born in 1959, and my daughter in 1961. Both of them are married. My daughter was divorced, though, but then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you lived in Samac your entire life, or rather, in the territory of the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1965 I lived in the village of Brvnik. I worked in Donja Slatina, later on in Samac. In 1965, I built a house in Bosanski Samac, and since then I have lived in Samac all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just speak a bit slower, if you possibly can. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what schools you have finished.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The higher school for work organization in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us briefly what you did during your career, just in a few words.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At first I worked as a bookkeeper. Then I was director of a cooperative. And then I worked as a commercial clerk at the agricultural combine there, and then I was head of a commercial department at the Agropromet company, until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of April, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Did you do your military service, and if so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service from 1951 until 1953. When I left the army, I got very sick and I was declared incapable -- permanently incapable of military service. Since 1953. And I have a military disability.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vukovic: Were you ever a member of any political party? When, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At first I was a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia and then a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And I remained one, and then, when the war broke out, I was still a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, I mean when we say "the war," we're talking about 1991, 1992, were you a member of any party then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time. I mean, except with the League of Communists. But these parties that were established at that time, no, I wasn't a member of any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any party now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A member of the socialist party of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber since when you've been a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now we are a bit more familiar with your curriculum vitae and now we'll move on to what this Trial Chamber is interested in. You lived in Samac in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are interested in the following here: Could you explain the atmosphere in Samac in a few sentences, in 1991 and the beginning of 1992. But I just ask you to speak slowly, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, as a retiree, I didn't have to go to work. I often strolled through town, I went to cafes, played cards, I went to the hotel pretty often. And in the second half of 1991, one could feel at the hotel, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, that is to say the market days in Samac, the restaurant would be full and one could see that people were sitting together according to party affiliations, and then we'd see that those who were in the HDZ wore the chequerboard sign in public. I and a friend of mine, Janko Bogdanovic, every Wednesday and Saturday, went to the hotel, sat there. We knew all these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Could one feel any divisions along ethnic lines, ethnic lines, in all these cafes, prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1990 I didn't notice anything of the kind, and not during the first half of 1991. But already during the second half of that year, when war had already broken out in Vukovar, was already going on in Vukovar, we in Samac could also feel such divisions along party lines. I used to sit all the time together in the company of Croats and Muslims, but no longer then, at that time. But the people who came to Samac from the villages started sitting at separate tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the Trial Chamber. You said it was market day on Wednesday and Saturday. Did people from the villages come to Samac on those days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: Did you walk around the villages? Did you go to the villages in Samac municipality in those days, and did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime towards the end of 1991 I did go into the various different villages, and while I still worked, my work was associated with these villages, and I knew all the people in the Croat and Serb villages. I actually knew more than 90 per cent of the heads of households in these villages. And I also went to visit my relatives in my native village. Sometime towards the end of 1991, at the exit from Tisina towards Grebnice --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter did not hear the end of the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So when I returned to Samac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes. Something is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Vukovic. You have to speak much, much slower, because the interpreters -- twice as slow as you're speaking because the interpreters can't follow. Please describe for us again what it was that you saw.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991 I went to my native village of Brvnik to visit my family, my wife's and my in-laws. This is the first time when I saw bags with sand on the -- alongside the road, at the entrance to Grebnice and the exit from Grebnice towards Brvnik. When I returned to Samac again, I spoke to Janko Bogdanovic, a friend of mine from Skarici, and I told him about these, and he told me: Ljubo, the people from Hasici have also set up such sandbags towards Hasici, the upper Gornji and Donji Hasici. This was the first time that I saw anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: The village of Grebnice and the village of Hasici, what was the predominant ethnicity of the villages there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Grebnice, 95 per cent or perhaps a bit over that were Croats, and there were also a few households of orthodox -- of the orthodox faith in Grebnice. And in Hasici, I think there were two or three households who were the Djurics, which is to say they were orthodox, and the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear in that period that in the town of Samac members of certain parties started arming themselves, the Muslims? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that they were being clandestinely armed, that -- that people of Muslim and Croat ethnicity were secretly arming themselves. And people said that weapons were being secretly brought into Bosnia across the River Sava, the bridge, and then they were distributing the weapons to their members. This is what I heard, and I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see or hear that there were any specially organised Muslim patrols organised on an ethnic principle in town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That I did see, and I also did see the auxiliary force of the police. They were armed. While these groups that patrolled in town at night, I did see him -- see them. I met them occasionally. They didn't ask me anything, nor ask me to do anything, because I had spent almost the entire year of 1992 in AS, the cafe of Miroslav Tadic, and I would stay there as long as -- until after midnight. And when I returned home after midnight, I would come across such patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm looking for some clarification too. He starts off by describing one group of patrols, then there's a statement about a second group of patrols, and then he says: "They were armed." And then: "These groups patrolled the town." Can we have some clarification of who was armed and who wasn't armed? Or is he saying all groups were armed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you will have to slow down. We will be having problems with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... notice here in the transcript and I believe this also needs some clarification. Here on line -- on page 19, line 2: "I had spent almost the entire year of 1992 in AS," which suggests that he actually lived at the cafe AS, which is not what the witness said, so maybe clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Vukovic. I will be asking you questions, so please wait a bit after my question and respond slowly. What patrols did you have in mind when you described that you had seen them when you returned home from the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Groups of unarmed Muslims patrolled in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this when you went to AS every day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was in the second half of 1991, and I was there every day in AS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: From the beginning of 1992 until the April events, did you also go to AS every day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since that day, or rather, night, when the attack, or rather, the war, started, I would be returning home at 7.30 in the evening. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you frequent the AS cafe regularly until that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the first months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to pursue this topic. I would like you to describe for the Trial Chamber the atmosphere in this AS cafe. But prior to that, just one question: How far is it to walk? How much time does it require to walk from AS to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is one kilometer and a half. That is the distance between my house and the AS cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What building, what important building, is near your house in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the electric power company. There used to be a dairy there and a municipal building, and after that it was the building of the electric power company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there in the vicinity of your house -- is the bridge on the River Sava in the vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is 500 meters from my house, and the harbour is also very near.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now proceed to talk about the atmosphere in the cafe AS. The end of 1991 and the first months of 1992, tell us, describe for the Trial Chamber what the atmosphere was like there and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In those months, in those days which I used to spend there entertaining myself, playing cards, in the section where the card players sat and in the other section near the door were the pool tables and other people who sat with their drinks and watched the pool players play. So the atmosphere was normal. We didn't feel any changes, we who were spending our time in the cafe except, except sometime around, I believe it was the end of March, or perhaps the beginning of March, I'm not sure. There was some sort of a commotion inside in that first part of the cafe, and we saw this person, this man, getting out a gun, a pistol. So he drew out his pistol and pointed it at a Muslim. And Brko immediately took him by the arm and led him out of the cafe and said: Don't you make any trouble here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So on several occasions, I think this happened two or three times, as far as I could notice, they came in groups, Alija Fitozovic, Omer Nalic, and Izet Izetbegovic, and a fourth person, a man was sitting with them. I don't know who he was. This was by the door where the entrance to this other room was. They were sitting there. They had had quite a lot to drink. And Alija started insulting someone, and I heard Omer -- I don't know whom, Omer Nalic warning him very, very seriously, telling him: Look, don't pick on these people. They are sitting here. They are relaxing. That is what I have come here to do, to relax. And don't do that. So we had incidents of this kind two or three times. He would get drunk and then he could not control himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please pause. Tell me of what ethnicity is Omer Nalic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Omer Nalic is a Muslim. He was the technical director in the electric power company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me about Mr. Izetbegovic. Did he hold any political office, any political function at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any political offices, but he was the vice-president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Omer Nalic often drop in the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not frequently. The other two did much more frequently. Omer Nalic liked to play cards, and Izet and this other guy, they didn't play cards. I never saw them playing cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a matter of clarification. On page 22, line 11, or line 10, the witness said: "He would get drunk and then he could not control himself." It is not quite obvious who is he referring to. Maybe my colleague can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Alija Fitozovic. Omer Nalic was warning him to behave properly and not to insult anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I have to complete my question before you start answering it, okay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we have cleared that up. So you have recounted two anecdotes for the Trial Chamber. Tell us: In that period, did the Muslims -- did Muslims and Croats and Serbs come to the AS cafe as the daily customers, guests of that cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time that I frequented this cafe, there were people playing with us cards, the same people: Musa Seric, a Muslim; Martin Benic, a Croat; Husic Ibrahim, a Muslim. They were with me together with me almost every day. I'm talking about card players.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vukovic: During the war - but please just reply with a yes or no and then we shall elaborate on it later - did you see any people in camouflage uniforms in Samac during the war, people that had come from Serbia, they called them special unit members? Did you see such people during the war in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war or before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when you saw them during the war in Samac, did you perhaps recall having ever seen them before the war in the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nor in Samac in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: What were the working hours of this cafe? From what time could go and sit there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't know what the actual working hours were. I sometimes would remain there until 3:00 in the morning, after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there any facility across the street from that cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the buildings of the former factory of knitted goods, and during the war it was a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Command of what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, are you aware that this was the command of the army of the 4th Detachment, that is, before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Leading question. Some issues, Your Honour, -- a lot of the facts I've hesitated to object on leading questions, but when we start to get to some important facts, they should be non--leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Contentious issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Vukovic, have you heard of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. My son was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the leaders, the senior officers, were of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of its setting up, I don't know who were its leaders, nor where its headquarters were. Later on I found out who the commander was, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When I found out, it was Radovan Antic who was commander, and Jovo Savic was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your son issued any weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your son go for some military exercises with that detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic composition was of that detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as my son told me, in the detachment there were Muslims and Croats as well. One of these Muslims is my son-in-law, my daughter's husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they also issued weapons? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to another subject now. Where were you on the 16th of April, 1992? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at AS for the entire afternoon. I came home at 7.30. I found my son at home. I said: Where is Mother? And he said: I've sent Mother off to the village to stay with relatives. I mean, I was sitting at the cafe. I didn't know what was going on. But I did not know what was going on in Samac that afternoon, and he was there and he realised that people were leaving town en masse. And then he said: I sent Mother away. And his wife had left earlier. He had driven her off to stay with her parents with the child. And my mother was already staying with her daughter in the village, so he had also sent his mother away, so I found him at home alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether before the war the citizens of Samac left town, went out of town? Did you notice that? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that. I also noticed it. It was obvious that during those last days before the war broke out, for the most part women and children were sent away to stay with relatives at villages so that they would not remain in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were women and children of all ethnic backgrounds leaving Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, but to what extent, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: You sat at the AS cafe. Was there anything unusual that afternoon or evening at the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing unusual. It was like any one of the previous days that I had spent there. That's the way it was that day too. Nobody was excited at the AS cafe. I think that these people who were together with me didn't know anything, just like I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall perhaps whether that evening there were any members of other ethnic groups in the AS cafe, or do you simply not remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same kind of people like every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything unusual when you came home in the evening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came home in the evening, it was already dark. Two neighbours came up and they asked me whether I would like to go to a place near my house where a man was selling beer, perhaps 50 meters away from my house. And I said I never went there for beer, and I'm not going there now either. Not much time went by and they came back and said to me: Ljubo, in the street of Dzemala Bjedica, there are 20 men, ethnic Muslims, who are out there with weapons. And I called my son and I said: Son, did you hear what they said? And he said: I do. And soon after that, Vukosav Acimovic came to our place. He's a neighbour. And he said: I'm on my own. Can I stay with the two of you? And we said: No problem what sorry. And the three of us sat there at our house. We sat there until the shooting started. I did not see these armed men. I just heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm looking for some clarification, if he could. He said he didn't see these men and he said they sat at their house. "We sat there until the shooting started." Is he indicating that these people were shooting within 10 or 15 minutes or what is -- could we have some clarification on that, please, the times and what's happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said that you did not see these men and that you stayed at home until the shooting started, what shooting did you mean? When did the shooting start?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The shooting started somewhere around 3.00 a.m., at the bridge. That's the shooting I meant. Not this in the evening, because these people were not shooting then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These neighbours, I mean in respect of these Muslims, you said that there were about 20 of them, did they tell you whether they were local people or some people who were unknown to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were local people. They were people from that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that the shooting started around 3.00 a.m. Did the shooting take place near your house? Did you hear shooting near your house or somewhere far away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that my house is about 100 to 150 meters away from the port, and the bridge is about 500 meters away, and that's where the shooting started, and we were in an awkward position. A war had broken out all of a sudden, for no good reason whatsoever. We were perplexed. We didn't get any sleep. We did not go out either. We just sat there at home and looked through the window until dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened at dawn?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When dawn started breaking -- I mean, there is a house in my neighbourhood that is eight meters away from my house. It's almost the same yard. We heard some noise, somebody said: Open up. We peered through the window and we saw a man dressed in a multicoloured uniform and we saw this man holding a gun like this. And it's right by the house. Another one right behind him, just like that. But this one walked in and he was banging at the door, and there was no one in the house. The third one also came up, and from the other side of the threshold, again he put his rifle up like this. And from our room where we were, we did not show up at all. They went out and they went to this other house across the street. That was a Muslim house, I mean the one where they went, I mean from this yard. And my son said: Daddy, should I call Meho? Perhaps he'll get into trouble. He phoned. Nobody answered the phone. Not long after that, the three of them returned to our yard, and my son went out to meet them and they ordered him to put his hands up. And I walked behind him. And he asked him: Have you got any weapons? And he said: Yes, I do. And then he asked: Are you a member of the detachment? He said: Yes, I am. And then he said: Your identity card. And he gave him his ID. Then he asked me whether I had my personal identity card there, and I showed him my identity card. And he asked: Was anybody else there? And yes, the neighbour Vukosav and then Vukosav --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt again, Your Honour. We have a lot of "he said" and some of them I think is his son and some I think is the person whose speaking to his son. Could he just use names, if he doesn't use the name of a person, could he use when his son speaks, his son's name so at least at some later point when we look at the transcript we can clarify who is speaking to who and who is saying what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put questions to you, and could you please answer those questions so that we would explain everything properly. A man came to your door --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not one. Three of them, in camouflage uniforms. And until then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you ever seen these three men before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of these three men address you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not me. They addressed my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the name of your son?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My son's name is Joco. He's the one that negotiated with them. They had those black caps, those black stockings on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This man in camouflage uniform, what did he say to Joco?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He said: Until further notice, no one is allowed to leave the yard. We will kill anyone who goes out into the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This man in camouflage uniform, did he ask Joco whether he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he ask Joco whether he was a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he ask Joco and you, and your neighbour, to show your identity cards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that now we managed to clarify this. Did Joco hand his rifle over to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He just said: Did you have any weapons? And he said: Yes. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they go to the neighbouring houses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Yes, they did, from one house to another, all in succession.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among your neighbours, were there any members of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Right next to my house was the house of an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this man a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they ask him whether he had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Croats and Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment, who you know were members of the 4th Detachment, were they asked to -- whether they had any weapons or to give them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They did not ask my son-in-law, and also they came to a Croat who was from the 4th Detachment before they came to my house. But no, they did not ask him for any weapons either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that day, did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We went out into the yard. We did not go out of the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any shooting during the day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All day, all day, incessantly. There was shooting at the bridge and over there in town. But at that time we could not know in town what was going on and where the shooting was taking place, but practically we were surrounded, as far as shooting is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, I mean the 17th of April, did you see or hear that an armoured vehicle had come into town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard, sometime in the afternoon, I heard sometime in the afternoon that a Praga had come to the port. Until then, I didn't even know what a Praga was, nor had I ever seen one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened? Tell us: What's the name of that part of town that you live in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That part of town is called the first quarter. But people call it Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened on the next day, on the 18th of April? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, we were at our house too. We could not go out anywhere. I sought the command, or rather, my son asked what would happen to him. He was not the only member of the 4th Detachment who was armed there. There were also some seven or eight other young men. And they could not get out. And they said: Just wait until further notice, don't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that day, did somebody come again to conduct a search or to look for weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that day, but the following day, on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the day I meant, the 18th of April. Is that right? That was that Saturday?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a brief description?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime around 12:00, during the day, two men, also in camouflage uniform, walked into my yard, and they asked me: Did somebody come to see you here yesterday morning? And I said: Yes. All right. Are there any Muslim houses here? Yes, there are, I said. And then: Where is the head of household? At Mico Sljokic's place, that's where he's sitting. Come with us. Only the men should go out. And then I was walking in front and the three of them got out. Meho, Mico, and Vaso Simic. And then they asked: Do you have any weapons? No. They didn't say anything else to them. Then we went to the gate and they said to me: We are going now. We are going around with a megaphone, around all the streets. And we are asking for those people who have weapons and who had not handed them in yet, do that, and nothing will happen to them. And then they started telling me about the Bicic brothers. I mean, this is what he said to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Just wait a second. I'm going to be putting questions to you. Who is the man who was telling you that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This man in camouflage uniform, I don't know. He was a Serbian. He was not from our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He told me: You don't know what you had in Samac. We were like brothers. Sorry. We went to the Bicic brothers, and I can tell you what we found in their house. So in this other inn, we found five machine-guns, ten rifles, three radio stations, sets, and bombs, grenades, and ammunition. So I told him, as far as I know, here in my house, nobody has -- nobody had any weapons, to the best of my knowledge. And indeed, there was nothing. And they didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to add: You said that this man in a camouflage uniform told you that they had found so much weapons in the brothers Bicic house that couldn't be put in three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Three passenger vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 33, line 19. The witness said "around my house," not "in my house."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said these houses -- these neighbours who were living around your house. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Vukovic, in his answer concerning these weapons and the Bicic brothers, he mentioned -- here we are. On line 17, that this man in the uniform, camouflage uniform, says that they had found certain things in the Bicic brothers' house. Then it goes on, the answer, and says: "So in this other inn." Now, we know, of course, they owned a pizza place. Where were the weapons found? In their accommodation, in their house, or in the pizza place, the inn, the cafe, whatever we like to call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, and this is not properly recorded in the transcript: "And also the innkeeper in the place of the innkeeper." That's what the witness said. He meant a third person, not the Bicic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Correction. Just a suggestion to correct the transcript. Page 33, line 17 and 18. In B/C/S language, witness testified that the other person told him that at the Bicic brothers they found five machine-guns. This is in transcript. Which is wrong. The witness said five heavy machine-guns and ten automatic rifles, which is very big difference in relation to what we have in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. The mike wasn't working. I think we should ask the witness and not have the attorneys testify. We have this witness saying first that they found something at the Bicic brothers, then in another inn they found something. Now, counsel, Mr. Lukic, just said, at line 34, line 14: "And also the innkeeper in the place of the innkeeper." That's what the witness said. He meant a third person, not the Bicic brothers." Now counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic is now mentioning that those items were found again at the Bicic brothers' house. That's not what the witness has said. Could we have the witness testify as to where these things -- or what information he received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Get the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think if we heard the tapes, we could establish what it was that the witness actually said. I didn't want to create any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you can see how we are having problems because the translators are really doing their best to do their work and follow what you are saying, but please slow down, because this is in our mutual interest. And please bear this in mind at all times. So tell us, please, slowly, what it was that you heard from this person, from this man. We have ample time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This man told me: You don't know what you had in Samac. Let me just tell you that in the place of the Bicic brothers, in their house, we found so much weapons that this could not be placed in three passenger vehicles. And in another place, Rajec's place, who keeps an inn next to the green market, there we found five heavy machine-guns and five rifles, grenades, mines, and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that that clears that up. You said five heavy machine-guns and ten automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do that day after that? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Then they left. I remained there. I returned to my yard, together with my son and the neighbour Vukosav and Vaso Simic, another neighbour of ours also came and he came there and stayed there and spent the night there with us in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take any decisions in the days that followed? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We kept looking for ways to get out. My sister has a flat, owns a flat in downtown, in the centre of town, but we couldn't reach that area. And there was no fighting. The war wasn't going on in the centre of town. And we were not allowed even to go out. It was only on Saturday evening that I and my son got out. I went to the flat and he went to this friend of his in Skarici. And on Sunday I went to Trivo Lukic's place, and his house is not far from my sister's flat. That was on Sunday. And on Sunday and the next three or four days I remained in Trivo Lukic's house. And my son returned only on Monday morning and reported to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During those days while you were at Trivo Lukic's place, his house, did you hear of any order having been issued in connection -- to the effect of any special conduct in terms of the life regime in the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of information? What was it that you heard? Did you actually leave his house at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The two of us, I and he, never left the house at all. His son drove around, bread and milk around the streets of Samac all day Sunday. And when he returned home -- but that day there was so much shooting over the Bosna and the railway tracks from the Slavonian side to the Samac side that one did not dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did he tell you? I mean the son of Trivo Lukic. What was it that he told you about the atmosphere in the city?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When he arrived, he told us that the situation was horrendous. He told -- no one actually dared move around Samac, because there was very heavy fighting going on. The tanks that had come there were placed near the Bosna, where the municipal court building is, and from there they opened fire. And from Prud they opened fire on Samac, so that one could not move about. And he just told us that the situation in Samac was terrible and he didn't say anything else when he came to the house in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, how many days, if you can recall, were you in the house of Trivo Lukic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was from Sunday morning until Thursday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to my sister's flat, and then I also went to see my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where did you spend the nights and the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I slept in my sister's flat, because she wasn't there and the flat was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it safer for you to spend the nights there, relative to your own flat?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the safest residential building in the town of Samac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, were you a member of the civil defence staff in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Trial Chamber how you became a member of the staff? Who called you to the staff? When was this, relative to the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the beginning of May. Trivo Lukic called me by phone and he told me to come to the premises of the local community, that I had been appointed a member of the civil defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you go there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whom did you find there? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I found Miroslav Tadic, Trivo Lukic, Aco Popovic, Mato Antunovic, Sveto [phoen] Ramusovic, Safet Hadzialijagic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please slow down. I'm very interested in this staff, so I'll ask you about each of these individuals. I will ask you right away: Did you find out who the commander of the civil defence staff was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Trivo Lukic, the man in whose place you had spent some time; is that not right? Will you tell us approximately how old he is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Trivo Lukic was born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Mato Antunovic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was he born, and of what ethnicity is he? Approximately the year.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact year in which Mato was born. He is much younger than me and he is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next person who you mentioned was Safet Hadzialijagic, known by the nickname of Pop. What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you maybe know whether he held any position in Samac prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the hotel manager, the hotel director, but I don't know in which time period exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ismet Ramusovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Aleksandar Popovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what year he was born, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zeljko Volasevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find him there in the civil defence staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what Zeljko Volasevic did before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko was a secretary of the local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were the premises of the staff to which you have come?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These were the premises which were being used which had been used by the local community, administration, prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: What was the popular name of the building in which the local community offices were in Samac? How did you call that building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The pensioners' building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Because below these local community offices which were on the first floor was a room which was used solely by pensioners and is still being used by them today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mato Antunovic and Safet Hadzialijagic, called Pop, leave Samac shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They left sometime in mid-May or the latter half of May. I don't remember the date. They both left. I know that Mato went to Belgrade, because his son was at the military academy there. And where Safet had gone, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Volasevic Zeljko also left the staff and Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Volasevic left much later, perhaps two or three months after they had departed. Zeljko then also left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: During those days, did you hear any stories from your friend in Skarici related to the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did. He phoned me one evening and he said to me: Could you come over to see me for a while? And I said to him: I will. Janko was his name. My wife and I went, and he said to me: Ljubo, these neighbours of mine from Hasici are going to Domaljevac en masse. And he said to me: That's why I called you. I don't know what this is, but they are going to Domaljevac en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when this was, relative to the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the last days of April or the first days of May. I'm not quite sure as to the date, but it was those days, around those days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: In the village of Hasici, did one ethnic group dominate among the population there? What was the population of Hasici? What was the predominant ethnicity there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that in the village of Hasici there were four houses in which Serbs lived and their last name was Djuric, and all the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to the civil defence staff, did you see whether there were some other services there on that floor, in that building, once you came there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came there, I found the people who worked for the Red Cross there as well. The premises right next door to ours were used by them. And right next to them was the room that was used by the social welfare centre. Those are the services that I found there then, and they remained there with us all the time, and we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your civilian protection staff, how many offices did it have there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We practically had one office, but we did use the office of secretary Zeljko Volasevic as well. So practically we had these two offices that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, on the ground floor of that building, there was another service too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Next to the premises of the pensioners' rooms are three other rooms. That is where the association of local fishermen was and of the local hunter society, and also the office of the veterans' association. Those three offices accommodated the service that was in charge of sending people out for work obligation. So they gathered there every day and they were sent out to work, to carry out their work obligation wherever they were supposed to go. But anyway, that's where they got their assignments. I don't know exactly where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown photographs D36 and D37/3. Could you please say whether that's the building that you've been talking about, the one that is called the pensioners' building.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could photograph D37 be placed on the ELMO now as well, please. Is this that same building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise that which is marked here with the red circle? What is it and what was it used for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The red circle goes around the mast where flags are put.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Do you remember whether there was a flag there during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout, while the Red Cross building was -- while the Red Cross was in this building, the Red Cross flag was placed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see an inscription at the entrance into this building, something that was of a discriminatory nature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lead, but I do have to put a question that stems from the Prosecution case. Did you ever see an inscription on that building stating that dogs, Muslims, and Croats were not allowed to enter that building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I went down there often to this group of people who were giving people work obligation assignments. I came to that building when I went to do my own work, and I never saw any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to move on to the activities of your staff of civilian protection. Tell me: What were the first things that you did during those first few days when you joined up? Just tell me what that was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When we gathered there, all of us, Miroslav Tadic then said to us what the tasks of the civilian protection staff were, and we made a plan as to how we should start. Our first job was to record goods at the facilities that belonged to companies whose seats were outside Bosanski Samac and also to make a list of goods in the shops that were privately owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Were these shops abandoned or were the owners of these privately owned shops still there in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to say, that Miroslav drew our attention to the fact that we should first go to those places for which it was known that the owners were no longer there, and also where perishable goods were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are these perishable goods?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All food products have an expiry date, and once the expiry date expires, then this can be very serious for the citizenry. There can be food poisoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a problem with agricultural pharmacies?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Agricultural pharmacies are a completely different thing. In addition to the seeds and fertilisers they sold, they also sold plant protection agents, so-called poisons. And Miroslav Tadic drew our attention to that fact, that the goods from those premises urgently had to be put into the warehouses of the agricultural combine. Perhaps a grenade could hit those shops and then the poison can affect all the citizens who happen to pass by there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Was there also a danger of these shops being broken into, looted? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely what Miroslav Tadic drew our attention to as well, because there was no one who took care about these facilities, these shops, and therefore goods had to be taken out of them as soon as possible and handed over to the warehouses of Velepromet, Velsanka, and the agricultural combine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How were these goods taken away? Was an inventory made or was everything taken away spontaneously? Did you know exactly what was taken where, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as this agreement was reached, upon Tadic's suggestion, we called a few persons, capable persons, who knew how to make inventories in stores. Pero Tovirac was one of them. For over 20 years, he was director of the Bosanka trading company at that time. He was a retired person as well. Then Cviko Tesic, also a salesperson, a retiree. We called him too. And Stevo Bozic. He was a worker at Mebos. But we called him in as a third member. So at that time, that was the first commission that started making the inventories of these goods, and they stayed there and they were the ones who made the largest number of inventories of goods. However, at these agricultural pharmacies, we engaged other persons, for the most part professionals. One of them is Djeto Dziskovic [phoen] who was an engineer of agriculture, then Vukosav Acimovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We don't need those details. Tell me: Where were those goods taken?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When the inventory was made, then the members of the commission came to us and said: We have finished the inventory. Now what? Then we had two trucks that had been made available to us, that had been assigned to us, precisely for the transport of these goods. Then we would go downstairs and we would ask that Kapetanovic, called Beg, to give us a few workers who would load the goods from these shops onto the trucks and then unload these goods at the warehouses of Velepromet and Bosanka. With these inventories, or rather, Pero Tovirac, the leader of the group, he carried the inventories, the lists, and he accompanied these goods. And then the warehouse clerk would sign the list, stating in this way that he had taken over the goods and then he would keep one copy and the other one would be taken to the municipality, to Ljubo Milic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many days did it take to finish that job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly how many days, but perhaps it was between 10 and 12 days, because there were quite a few shops for which we had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In your opinion, how many shops were involved in this making of inventories?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of these shops that sold industrial goods, but we had three agricultural pharmacies that were well stocked indeed. And the owner was Agrokop Novi Sad, Seme from Belgrade, and Zmaj from Zemun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: These three pharmacies that you mentioned, from which entity or from which republic do the owners come from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I've said just now that the owner of one of the pharmacies was Agrokop from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Novi Sad is in Vojvodina, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say another thing, that it was in a private home of some man called Ravo. All right. Then Seme from Belgrade, its seat is in Belgrade, in Serbia. Then Zmaj from Zemun. That's a factory that manufactures agricultural machinery. It is in Zemun, but they had a pharmacy, an agricultural pharmacy in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You said three pharmacies. Can you tell us approximately how many shops were included during those ten days or so, just to give an approximation to the Trial Chamber. We don't have to go into details.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, I would say, 15 or 16 shops, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff, after that, did it ever make any inventories of any shops anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When we finished this job with these shops, we didn't do any such thing anymore, because it wasn't necessary. These other shops were actually run by the companies that had their seats in Samac, so they could take care of it themselves. It is not that we from the civilian protection staff would have to interfere in this in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the inventory of these shop -- I'm now going to ask you about all of this in chronological order, but I'm going to deal with individual topics because there are quite a few of them, but I think that this also pertains to this first period of the war. Correct me if I'm wrong. Was there a problem that involved shelters in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it did. Of course there was a problem, because there was shelling, there were combat operations, and Samac was unprepared as far as shelters were concerned. There was one single building, the one that I said was the safest one in Samac. That is where there were over 280 persons in the basement. In order to make it possible for people to seek shelter from shells as soon as possible, Tadic gave an assignment to all of us, all members of the civilian protection staff, to tour the entire town of Samac and to see what can be done and to equip the shelters as much as possible so that people could come as soon as possible to seek shelter from shells. We toured all of this, we saw it, we returned. We wrote signs saying "shelter." And we put the distance on the signs, stating how far away the nearest shelter was. Until the present day, there are such signs in Samac stating how far away shelters are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the only, so to say, real shelter was the one that you described. Let me ask you one question: Are you aware of the fact that that shelter and life in it was organised by Mr. Marko Kuresevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. It was Marko Kuresevic who organised it and set up the records of people who had sought shelter there. He also put the orderlies on the doors, and no one could enter into the building. Can you imagine someone coming there and throwing a bomb there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, just for the sake of the Trial Chamber's finding out: Where is this building relative to the pensioners' club, to the pensioners' building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This building is some 10 meters away from the pensioners' centre, and I forgot to say that Marko Kuresevic immediately went to Miroslav Tadic to tell him what he had done and what organizational measures he had undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the war anyone had been killed by a shell or suffered any injury on account of a shell in the immediate vicinity of the pensioners' centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I don't know what date this was, but this was about 10:00 a.m. when the shells started landing on Samac, and right across from this building, in the direction of the -- was the -- was the shop, the store of Bosanka, the trading company, and Refika Pisarevic worked there, so a shell landed on it and killed her. Also on the same day a Muslim boy was killed by the municipal building. His father's name, or rather, his father was called Bibe Ranko. He was not killed on the spot, but he succumbed to his injuries very shortly after getting hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a civil defence staff, were you able of ordering any citizen to go into a shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't order anyone, but we informed all the citizens where these shelters were, for them to see which was the nearest one to them in the event of shelling, so they could indeed seek shelter in them. We were in no position to issue any orders to anyone. And of course, we didn't know when the shelling would start either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you -- could you, as civil defence staff, forbid anyone to leave a shelter if that someone wanted to go home from it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see how we could have done that, forbidden anyone. If we didn't know that anyone was in the shelter. Actually, our duty was to inform the citizens were the shelters were and as to whether they would flee from the shelters, that was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: Did you encounter any problems during the war in Samac with unexploded mines, and did your staff have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally had been reported about such incidents on a couple of occasions that a shell had landed, namely, and that it hadn't exploded. Marko would come and inform me: This spot has been marked. I would immediately inform the command brigade in Pelagicevo by telephone, because they had a demining expert units situated there. And they would send personnel to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are aware of the remaining time for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in my third and fourth submissions that I would be interrogating this witness between four hours, and I believe that I will be able to finish within three or four hours. I will not go into much detail. I just want to finish the topic of civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first witness who has provided any information on the civil defence, so we would have no objection to counsel bringing out some testimony on this civil defence, or civil protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as long as he does that within the time allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My topics will be associated solely with civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many telephones did you have in the civil defence staff that were operational?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many telephones were operational in that building, generally speaking, during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just that one telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who minded that telephone? Who sat by that telephone as a rule?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All of us members of the civil defence staff, when we didn't leave the premises, we would be there. We would take turns. I would be the one who would spend most of the time there, as well as Ismet Ramusovic and Zeljko Volasevic, while he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Who called you on the phone, and who did people want to speak to relative to the existing services in that building? Was the civil defence the only one who used the phone? Would you tell us a bit about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After the telephone lines went down in town, there remained just several operational telephones, the one in the Executive Board, the one that we had, the one in the post office and in the secretariat of defence, as far as I know, and this telephone was used not only by those who assigned the workers, but we had lots of problems. Every time someone called in respect of a problem connected with the assignment of workers and the service, I had to transmit such messages to the effect that someone was looking for a worker. I would go to go down, convey the message to them, and return upstairs. In addition to that, when families left Samac, all the people crowded in to use our phone, because they didn't know where the families were. They wanted to establish contact to seek their families. So it was a general rush on our phone. The only one operational phone which the citizenry could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this first part of your story in more detail. Did this Kapetanovic, whom you mentioned, and these people who worked as the desk officers for assigning people to work duty, did they have any other contact with the, so to speak, outside world, except by way of your telephone, the telephone connection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the requests placed via your telephone? What kind of information was required through you by that phone? Please describe this for us. Give us an example, in fact.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had instances of several workers being required to go and work somewhere, and they had no telephone connection, so they would transmit to us to convey to them how many workers were needed, where these workers were needed, so we would convey this message to them downstairs, and that was, as far as we were concerned, we had to receive such messages and we had to transmit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So whatever messages you were given by phone, you had to relay to them. But tell us: Who was they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic and then -- while he was there, and then Mr. Celic and after Celic it was Misic. So they took turns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to relaying these messages, did you do -- have anything to do with the work duty service people as civil defence staff, apart from the relaying of messages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The relationship that we had with them was such that whenever we needed some intervention on a certain facility, as a matter of urgency, then we would ask them whether they could make their men available to us for such repairs, or rather, remedial action to be undertaken. So these were the personal contacts that we had on a personal basis between the civil defence staff members and them, as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness be shown a document now which I wish to tender into evidence, which is marked PDB 20/3. [In English] 20/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you take a -- you can in fact take a look at it directly or on the ELMO, as you wish. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is -- I am. I am familiar. I wrote this document. And Miroslav Tadic signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify for us approximately for which month was this payroll list drawn up or, as we put it, for remuneration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was for the month of May. I can see that where I wrote that Tesic Stojan received a salary for April in his unit, because he was in the army, then -- and then we took him over, withdrew him from the unit in order to drive goods for the needs of the staff and to be available for the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me about this Ismet Hurtic. It also says "driver" here. Of what ethnicity was this person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they then as drivers work on something else, on a different job associated with the civil defence staff? What was this truck of the civil defence used for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ismet Hurtic was mainly engaged working for the Red Cross and this was his own private car. But for the needs of the civil defence staff, he mainly transported coffins to the morgue and the dead to the cemeteries at which their funerals were to take place. This was his job where the civil defence staff were concerned. Otherwise he worked for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says in this document Miroslav Tadic will be paid out in the Crisis Staff. Do you know anything about that? Was Tadic a member of the Crisis Staff? Do you know that? And did he receive his salary in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff, nor did I ever ask him about whether he was a member. But I do know that he went to sessions and he told me to write this the way it is written and that he would be paid out there and to tell the person drawing up the list, the payroll list with the amounts to be paid out, that he was also to be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need this document any longer. Can we please now go into private session, because I would like to put a few questions to the witness. But before that, can we please be assigned a number for this document, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D106/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion see Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the civilian protection have any role in securing a water supply for the hospital during those days, and why was it so?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no power in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before the answer: When you asked the witness a question whereby he had to mention two of the accused persons, did you want that to be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please continue telling us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no power in all of town. The water supply could not function. Then also the aggregates could not work. The first day or two we had to provide water in trucks from the artesian wells from the villages around. Very soon the water supply aggregates started working, and then in the morning and in the evening, water would be put into the water trucks and one water truck would be by the hospital. It would be there for the haemodialysis department. And the other one at the kitchen at Tekstilac. And that is the way it was done every morning and every evening. These water trucks were filled and then the aggregate would go on, because there was not enough fuel for it to work all the time. So then the water trucks would be loaded and then they would stop working, the aggregates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who organised this particular work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the civilian protection staff need a plumber, and if so, who did that particular work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC
